title: Proteins
content: Proteins are essential macronutrients made up of amino acids. They are crucial for building and repairing tissues, making enzymes and hormones, and supporting immune function. Good sources include lean meats, fish, eggs, dairy products, legumes, and tofu. The recommended daily intake is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight for sedentary adults, increasing to 1.2-2.0 grams for active individuals. Complete proteins contain all nine essential amino acids, while incomplete proteins lack one or more. Combining plant proteins can provide complete amino acid profiles.

title: Carbohydrates
content: Carbohydrates are the body's primary energy source. They are classified into simple carbs (sugars) and complex carbs (starches and fiber). Complex carbohydrates from whole grains, vegetables, and legumes provide sustained energy and essential nutrients. The glycemic index (GI) measures how quickly foods raise blood sugar levels. Low-GI foods are preferable for stable energy. Adults should aim for 45-65% of calories from carbohydrates, with emphasis on fiber-rich sources. Minimum recommended fiber intake is 25 grams for women and 38 grams for men daily.

title: Dietary Fats
content: Dietary fats are essential for hormone production, nutrient absorption, and cell membrane integrity. Fats are categorized as saturated, unsaturated (mono and poly), and trans fats. Unsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts, avocados, and fatty fish are heart-healthy. Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) from fatty fish reduce inflammation and support brain health. Saturated fats should be limited to less than 10% of daily calories. Trans fats should be avoided entirely. Total fat intake should comprise 20-35% of daily calories.

title: Vitamin D
content: Vitamin D is crucial for calcium absorption, bone health, and immune function. It is produced by the skin when exposed to sunlight and found in fatty fish, fortified dairy, and egg yolks. Many people are deficient, especially in northern climates. The recommended daily intake is 600-800 IU, though some experts suggest higher doses. Deficiency can lead to weakened bones, increased infection risk, and mood disorders. Blood levels of 30-50 ng/mL are considered optimal. Supplementation may be necessary for those with limited sun exposure.

title: Vitamin B12
content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nerve function, DNA synthesis, and red blood cell formation. It is found naturally only in animal products including meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. Vegans and vegetarians must supplement or consume fortified foods. Deficiency can cause anemia, neurological problems, and fatigue. The recommended daily intake is 2.4 micrograms for adults. Absorption decreases with age, so older adults may need higher doses or injections. Methylcobalamin and cyanocobalamin are common supplement forms.

title: Iron
content: Iron is vital for oxygen transport in blood and energy metabolism. Heme iron from animal sources is more easily absorbed than non-heme iron from plants. Good sources include red meat, poultry, fish, legumes, and fortified cereals. Vitamin C enhances iron absorption, while calcium and tannins inhibit it. Women of reproductive age need 18 mg daily, while men need 8 mg. Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide, causing anemia and fatigue. Excess iron can be toxic, so supplementation should be approached carefully.

title: Mediterranean Diet
content: The Mediterranean diet is based on traditional eating patterns of countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea. It emphasizes olive oil as the primary fat source, abundant fruits and vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds. Fish and seafood are consumed regularly, while red meat is limited. Moderate wine consumption with meals is traditional. This diet is associated with reduced cardiovascular disease, lower inflammation, and improved cognitive function. It is rich in antioxidants, fiber, and healthy fats. The diet promotes social eating and mindful food enjoyment.

title: Ketogenic Diet
content: The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, very low-carbohydrate eating plan that puts the body into ketosis. Carbohydrates are limited to 20-50 grams daily, forcing the body to burn fat for fuel. Macronutrient ratios are typically 70-75% fat, 20-25% protein, and 5-10% carbohydrates. The diet can promote rapid weight loss and improve blood sugar control. Foods include meats, fatty fish, eggs, butter, cheese, nuts, and low-carb vegetables. Potential side effects include keto flu, constipation, and nutrient deficiencies. Long-term sustainability and safety require medical supervision.

title: Vegan Diet
content: A vegan diet excludes all animal products including meat, fish, dairy, eggs, and honey. It relies on plant-based protein sources like legumes, tofu, tempeh, seitan, and plant-based meat alternatives. Whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds form the foundation. Critical nutrients to monitor include vitamin B12, vitamin D, omega-3 fatty acids, iron, zinc, and calcium. Supplementation is typically necessary for B12. When well-planned, vegan diets can meet all nutritional needs and may reduce risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers.

title: Paleo Diet
content: The Paleo diet mimics the eating patterns of our prehistoric ancestors, focusing on whole, unprocessed foods. It includes lean meats, fish, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds while excluding grains, legumes, dairy, refined sugar, and processed foods. Proponents claim it aligns with human genetic evolution. Benefits may include weight loss, improved blood lipids, and better blood sugar control. Critics note that it excludes nutritious food groups and may be difficult to sustain long-term. The diet is high in protein and fiber but may be low in calcium and vitamin D.

title: Balanced Meal Composition
content: A balanced meal includes all macronutrient groups in appropriate proportions. The plate method suggests filling half your plate with vegetables, one quarter with lean protein, and one quarter with whole grains or starchy vegetables. Include a source of healthy fat like olive oil, avocado, or nuts. Aim for colorful variety to ensure diverse nutrient intake. Meals should provide sustained energy without causing blood sugar spikes. Preparation in advance through meal prepping can improve dietary adherence. Consider individual caloric needs based on age, sex, activity level, and health goals.

title: Meal Timing and Frequency
content: Meal timing can affect metabolism, weight management, and energy levels. Traditional advice suggests three main meals with optional snacks. Intermittent fasting approaches limit eating to specific time windows, such as 16:8 (16 hours fasting, 8 hours eating). Eating breakfast may benefit some individuals but is not essential for everyone. Avoid large meals close to bedtime for better sleep quality. Post-workout nutrition within 30-60 minutes supports muscle recovery. Consistent meal times help regulate hunger hormones and circadian rhythms. Individual responses to meal timing vary significantly.

title: Weight Loss Fundamentals
content: Sustainable weight loss requires a moderate caloric deficit of 500-750 calories daily, resulting in 1-1.5 pounds lost per week. Protein intake should be prioritized to preserve muscle mass during weight loss. Aim for 0.7-1 gram of protein per pound of body weight. High-fiber foods increase satiety and reduce overall calorie intake. Avoid drastic restrictions that are unsustainable. Focus on whole, nutrient-dense foods rather than processed diet products. Regular physical activity enhances fat loss and metabolic health. Tracking food intake increases awareness and accountability.

title: Diabetic-Friendly Diet
content: Managing diabetes through diet involves controlling blood sugar levels through carbohydrate management. The glycemic index and glycemic load help identify foods that cause minimal blood sugar spikes. Focus on fiber-rich complex carbohydrates, lean proteins, and healthy fats. Distribute carbohydrate intake evenly throughout the day. Limit added sugars and refined grains. The plate method works well for diabetics: half non-starchy vegetables, quarter lean protein, quarter whole grains. Regular meal timing helps maintain stable blood sugar. Work with a registered dietitian for personalized guidance.

title: Heart-Healthy Diet
content: A heart-healthy diet reduces cardiovascular disease risk through specific dietary choices. Limit saturated fat to less than 7% of calories and eliminate trans fats. Increase omega-3 fatty acids from fatty fish eaten twice weekly. Reduce sodium intake to less than 2,300 mg daily, ideally 1,500 mg. Emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes for fiber and antioxidants. Choose lean proteins and plant-based options. Limit red meat and processed meats. The DASH diet and Mediterranean diet are evidence-based approaches for heart health.

title: Eggs Nutritional Profile
content: Eggs are highly nutritious, providing complete protein with all essential amino acids. One large egg contains 6 grams of protein, 5 grams of fat, and 77 calories. Eggs are rich in choline for brain health, B vitamins, and vitamin D. The yolk contains most nutrients including healthy fats and antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin for eye health. Recent research indicates dietary cholesterol in eggs has minimal impact on blood cholesterol for most people. Eggs can be part of a healthy diet, with most guidelines allowing up to 3 eggs daily.

title: Salmon Nutritional Profile
content: Salmon is one of the most nutritious foods available, particularly rich in omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA. A 3.5-ounce serving provides 25 grams of high-quality protein and over 2 grams of omega-3s. Wild-caught salmon is generally leaner with fewer contaminants than farmed varieties. Salmon is an excellent source of vitamin D, B vitamins, selenium, and astaxanthin. Regular consumption is associated with reduced inflammation, improved heart health, and better cognitive function. Aim to eat fatty fish like salmon at least twice per week.

title: Spinach Nutritional Profile
content: Spinach is a nutrient-dense leafy green vegetable with minimal calories. It provides vitamin K for blood clotting, vitamin A for vision, folate for cell division, and iron for oxygen transport. Spinach contains antioxidants including lutein, zeaxanthin, and beta-carotene. Raw spinach is high in oxalates which can inhibit calcium and iron absorption; cooking reduces oxalate content. One cup of raw spinach provides 7 calories, 1 gram of protein, and 1 gram of fiber. It can be eaten raw in salads or cooked in various dishes.

title: Hydration and Water Intake
content: Adequate hydration is essential for all bodily functions including temperature regulation, nutrient transport, and waste removal. General recommendations suggest 8 cups (64 ounces) of water daily, though individual needs vary based on activity level, climate, and body size. Thirst is not always a reliable indicator of hydration status. Urine color should be pale yellow. All beverages contribute to hydration, though water is calorie-free and ideal. Fruits and vegetables also contribute to water intake. During exercise or hot weather, increase fluid intake and consider electrolyte replacement for extended activity.

title: Dietary Supplements
content: Dietary supplements can fill nutritional gaps but should not replace a balanced diet. Common supplements include multivitamins, vitamin D, omega-3 fish oil, and probiotics. Certain populations may benefit from specific supplements: B12 for vegans, iron for menstruating women, folic acid for pregnant women. Quality varies significantly between brands; look for third-party testing certifications like USP or NSF. Some supplements can interact with medications or have side effects at high doses. Consult healthcare providers before starting supplementation, especially for fat-soluble vitamins that can accumulate in the body.
